--- title: "08 — DARM calibration via Pintelon–Schoukens" description: "A measurement-design study: a Pintelon–Schoukens-optimal DARM calibration-line scheme reaches the Advanced-LIGO O3/O4 random-error (response-uncertainty) levels with far less injected amplitude and time than the standard fixed-line scheme — ~18× less injected energy (≈4× less amplitude, or ~18× less time) — and turns the amplitude↔time trade into a Pareto slider for designing the cal strategy at any target precision down to 0.1%." image: thumbnails/08.svg categories: [calibration, closed-loop, DARM] freeze: true --- ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"} ## Abstract Calibration lines cost the detector **amplitude** (injected onto the mirrors, competing with astrophysical strain) and **time**. This is a measurement-design study of how to spend both as frugally as possible. Applying **Pintelon–Schoukens optimal excitation** to the DARM loop — choosing where to put the lines and how to split the drive to minimise the Cramér–Rao bound on the seven time-dependent calibration factors (TDCFs) — a P&S-optimal scheme reaches the published Advanced-LIGO **O3/O4 random-error levels** (the statistical part of the response budget) with **~18× less injected energy** than the standard fixed-line scheme (≈4× less amplitude, or ~18× less time) and **>1000× less** than a naive broadband injection. Because the response error scales as `1/√(amplitude²·time)`, the amplitude↔time trade is a **Pareto slider**: pick a target random-error level — O3, O4, or a 0.1% stretch — and read off the gentlest/fastest campaign that reaches it. The twin uses the coupled detuned-cavity sensing (SRC detuning splits the cavity pole into a complex pair) and hierarchical M0/PUM/ESD actuation, matching the Sun 2020 O3 parameterisation. ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## What you'll learn - **The thesis:** reach O3/O4 random-error levels **gentler and faster** with Fisher-optimal lines, and design the campaign on an **amplitude↔time Pareto slider** (down to 0.1%). - The multisine pipeline applied to the **gravitational-wave readout** (DARM): recovering `C` and the per-stage actuation `κ` leakage-free, with `1/√T` convergence onto the Cramér–Rao bound. - **Hierarchical actuation across the quad** (M0/PUM/ESD), the inter-stage crossovers, and the **calibration lines at their real height in the DARM spectrum**. - **Fisher-optimal line design** — placement + drive split (with the SRC detuning that splits the cavity pole), benchmarked head-to-head against the LIGO O3/O4 line schemes. - **The response-error budget & Pareto** — propagating the cal-line CRB into `δR/R(f)` and mapping the amplitude/time cost to reach each random-error level. ::: [![Launch in Binder](https://mybinder.org/badge_logo.svg)](https://mybinder.org/v2/gh/CaltechExperimentalGravity/system_ident/HEAD?urlpath=lab/tree/docs/examples/08-darm-calibration.ipynb) · run this page live (no install; the [in-browser demo](interactive.qmd) is instant) The earlier examples identify suspensions. This one identifies the **gravitational-wave readout itself** — the DARM loop a LIGO calibration group characterises every run. The method does not change: a periodic multisine, a leakage-free reference FRF, a measured per-bin noise model, and a Cramér–Rao envelope. Only the plant is new: a closed loop with a sensing function `C`, three-stage actuation `A`, and a digital servo `D`, under **both** process disturbance and readout noise. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Representative, not a specific interferometer The twin uses representative Advanced-LIGO numbers — a coupled-cavity pole near 360 Hz, a ~77 µs delay, three pendulum-stage actuators, and a UGF≈50 Hz loop. It is a *demonstration* of the measurement, not a calibration of any real instrument. The page is rendered with `freeze: true`. ::: ::: {#1e1cfb73 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Setup — import the presentation glue"} import sys, pathlib _p = pathlib.Path.cwd() for _c in [_p, *_p.parents]: if (_c / "docs" / "darm_demo.py").exists() and str(_c / "docs") not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c / "docs")) if (_c / "darm_demo.py").exists() and str(_c) not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c)) import numpy as np import darm_demo as dd ``` ::: ## The loop and what calibration delivers DARM strain is `h = R·d_err/L` with response `R = (1+G)/C` and open-loop gain `G = A·D·C`. The calibration job is to know `R(f)` — and, underneath it, the sensing `C` and the three actuation strengths — to ~1 % in magnitude and ~1° in phase across the band. ::: {#e16abaa2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="The twin's truth — C, A, G, R"} dd.truth_fig() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## One Pcal multisine — what you'd watch A single periodic multisine injected at Pcal, ramped on and off over 3 s, with the DARM error read out under the loop's real disturbance and readout noise. ::: {#7d844b88 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Raw Pcal measurement — drive in, d_err out"} a = dd.pcal_audit(seed=1) dd.pcal_timeseries_fig(a) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The leakage-free FRF `d_err/x_pc = C/(1+G)` with its per-line coherence, on the analytic truth: ::: {#82aae87d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Leakage-free FRF + coherence"} dd.pcal_bode_fig(a) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## The deliverable: R(f), model-free Because `d_err/x_pc = C/(1+G)`, the response is simply its reciprocal — `R(f) = 1/FRF`, with no model in the loop. Its CRB envelope falls straight out of the FRF's per-bin error. ::: {#c59149a8 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Recovered R(f) ± CRB vs truth"} dd.response_envelope_fig(a) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Underneath: the sensing function C Multiplying the FRF by the (known, designed) loop factor `(1+G)` exposes the optical sensing `C`; a weighted complex fit returns the optical gain, the coupled-cavity pole, and the delay. ::: {#a3d220b9 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Sensing fit — g_C, f_cc, τ"} from IPython.display import display display(dd.sensing_table(a)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Sensing function C — representative truth vs P&S recovery** | sensing parameter | true | recovered | σ (CRB) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | optical gain g_C [ct/m] | 1e+06 | 1e+06 | 2.6e+02 | | cavity pole f_cc [Hz] | 360.00 | 359.94 | 0.15 | | delay τ [µs] | 77.0 | 76.9 | 0.06 | ::: ::: ## The actuation strengths, Pcal as the ruler A Pcal-only measurement cannot separate the three stages (they live inside `G` as a product). Driving each stage in turn and dividing by the Pcal FRF removes `C/(1+G)`, leaving `κ_i N_i` referenced to the absolute Pcal meter — so each `κ` comes back on its own. ::: {#b123abdd .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Recover κ_U / κ_PU / κ_T"} d = dd.actuation_campaign(seed=2) display(dd.actuation_table(d)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Actuation strengths κ — Pcal as the absolute ruler** | stage | true κ | recovered κ | σ (CRB) | |Δ| | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | UIM | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.00062 | 0.01% | | PUM | 0.400 | 0.399 | 0.0013 | 0.24% | | TST | 0.080 | 0.077 | 0.007 | 3.55% | ::: ::: ## How fast does each parameter converge? The number a calibration group actually plans around is *exposure* — how long a measurement must run to pin each parameter to a target. Because the estimator is period-averaged, every parameter's variance falls as `1/P` (equivalently `1/T`), and the fit / period-to-period-variance σ **is** the Cramér–Rao bound — so the recovered 1σ tracks the `1/√T` law with no free knob. Below, the six core calibration parameters — sensing `g_C`, `f_cc`, `τ` and the three actuator strengths `κ_UIM`, `κ_PUM`, `κ_TST` — are recovered at `P = 16…128` periods and their fractional 1σ plotted against record length. All six fall parallel to the dashed `1/√T` reference; the vertical spread is just per-parameter SNR (`κ_TST`, the weakest actuator, sits highest). Read off the exposure for a target: e.g. sub-1 % on every strength inside a ~minute-scale record here. ::: {#dc764aa2 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="σ(θ)/θ vs record length for every cal parameter, against the CRB"} dd.convergence_fig() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Hierarchical actuation and the crossovers the cal lines measure DARM is actuated on all four quad masses hierarchically: the fast, weak ESD (**TST**) takes the command directly, and two nested offload filters push the low-frequency drive up the chain to the **PUM** and the strong, slow **M0** (top mass). Each stage's DARM-referred authority is `A_i = κ_i · D_i(f) · N_i(f)` — the M0-damped reduced-QUAD compliance `N_i` shaped by the distribution filter `D_M0 = O_A·O_B`, `D_PUM = O_A`, `D_TST = 1`. The offload runs in *force* units, so the compliances carry the hierarchy and `κ_i = 1`. M0 owns the lowest frequencies and hands off up the chain, so adjacent stages cross where their authority is equal — **M0/PUM near `F_PT ≈ 0.5 Hz`, PUM/TST near `F_EP ≈ 10 Hz`**. Those crossovers are exactly what a per-stage calibration line on each actuator measures (see `darm_tv.cal_line_response`). The 0.4–3 Hz peaks are the L1/L2/L3 forest, undamped by the M0-only local loop — the twin's real L1 ETMX damping, faithful to the plant. ::: {#2c910afc .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Per-stage actuation |A_i(f)| with the M0/PUM and PUM/TST crossovers"} dd.hierarchical_actuation() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Future upgrade — damped quad plants from `ssprescale`"} The M0-damped compliances here are built from the reduced QUAD plus a reproduction of the twin's L1 ETMX M0-only velocity damping. A future upgrade will instead use the **new damped quad plants vendored by the `ssprescale` package** (work in progress) — a properly-scaled, multi-loop (M0 + L1 + L2) damped suspension model — so the in-band compliances and the exact crossover frequencies come from the production damping design rather than a single-loop M0 stand-in. ::: ## The calibration lines in the DARM spectrum In operation the strengths are tracked *continuously* by always-on calibration lines — one per actuation stage, plus a Pcal reference — not swept campaigns. What matters is how far each line stands above the DARM noise, because the per-record strength precision is `σκ/κ ≈ 1/SNR`. Below, one line per stage (M0 low, PUM mid, TST in-band) is injected on the hierarchical twin, the loop is simulated under its length-disturbance + readout floor, and the DARM error is deconvolved back to displacement `x = d_err·(1+G)/C`. The spectrum is a full-record periodogram (resolution `df = 1/T`), so **each line stands exactly its SNR above the floor** — the number read straight off the plot. The floor is `√(disturbance² + (readout/|C|)²)`: flat length noise at low frequency, rising above the cavity pole where readout noise divided by the shrinking `|C|` takes over. Longer integration lifts every line as `√T`. ::: {#54523aeb .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Inject per-stage cal lines; simulate + deconvolve to a calibrated DARM spectrum"} cs = dd.cal_line_spectrum() dd.cal_line_spectrum_fig(cs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#739cf671 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Per-line height, SNR, and the strength precision it buys"} display(dd.cal_line_table(cs)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Per-stage calibration lines: displacement amplitude, in-record SNR, and the per-record strength precision (≈ 1/SNR). Longer integration scales SNR as √T.** | stage line | f [Hz] | displacement [m rms] | SNR (256 s) | σκ/κ [%] | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | M0 | 0.45 | 2.25e-17 | 90 | 1.11 | | PUM | 3.00 | 3.5e-17 | 140 | 0.71 | | TST | 40.00 | 5.96e-19 | 260 | 0.38 | ::: ::: ## Sizing the lines: 0.1% on every parameter in under 5 minutes The lines above were placed by hand. The right question is the Pintelon–Schoukens one: **where should the lines sit, and how big should they be, to measure every calibration parameter to a target precision in a target time?** We estimate seven parameters — the sensing TDCFs `κ_C`, `f_cc`, the SRC detuning `δ` and delay `τ`, and the three actuation strengths `κ_M0`, `κ_PUM`, `κ_ESD` (these define the loop through `C` and `A = Σ κ_i N_i`, exactly the O3/O4 model of [Sun et al. 2020](https://dcc.ligo.org/public/0162/P1900245/007/CalO3.pdf)). Each line's closed-loop FRF is measured against the DARM noise floor with `SNR = a·√T/√S_x`; the Fisher matrix on the (log) parameters is the standard `Γ = Σ 2·SNR²·Re[∂lnH*·∂lnH]`, and the CRB is `Γ⁻¹`. We place the line frequencies and split the total drive to **minimise the worst parameter's fractional σ** (so the slowest-converging parameter governs), then read off the time each reaches 0.1%. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## The coupled SRC model: the cavity pole splits The sensing `C` here is the **coupled** detuned-cavity response `C ∝ 1/(1 + i f/f_cc − A·sin(2δ)·(f/f_cc)²)`: at tuning it is the single real cavity pole, and as the SRC detunes the pole **splits into a complex-conjugate pair** (colliding near δ≈7°; anti-restoring on the other sign) — not a separate low-frequency spring factor. That physical `δ` is one of the parameters the lines must pin. ::: ::: {#d832cbea .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Fisher-optimal line sizing + O3/O4 comparison (differential evolution)"} sz = dd.cal_sizing(seed=0) dd.convergence_to_target_fig(sz) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Every parameter reaches 0.1% well before the 5-minute mark (all inside ~90 s here). The SRC detuning `δ` and the weak upper actuators `κ_TST`/`κ_PUM` are the slowest — `δ` needs high-frequency information where the readout floor is worst, and those stages carry less authority — while `κ_C`, `f_cc` and `κ_M0` are fast. The lines land where the physics puts them (below). The **Pcal (sensing) line frequencies are Fisher-placed** — each where its parameter is most informative: `f_cc` near the cavity pole, `δ` and `τ` high (the coupled-cavity `f²` split-curvature and the delay phase both grow with `f`). The **actuator line frequencies follow the actuation hierarchy** — each stage is measured in its own authority band (M0 low, PUM mid, ESD ~tens of Hz), where that stage's DARM-referred response `D_i·N_i` is largest so the ruler `H_stage/H_pcal = κ_i·D_i·N_i` carries the most SNR. (Crowding all three actuator lines into one shared mid-band region, as the fixed-line schemes do, starves the slow upper stages — that is exactly where the head-to-head below shows the biggest gap.) The total drive is then split to balance the worst-parameter time-to-0.1%. ::: {#34128736 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Where the sized lines sit over the DARM floor"} dd.sized_lines_fig(sz) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Head-to-head with LIGO O3/O4 At **equal total drive**, how does this Fisher-optimal placement compare to the actual O3 and O4 calibration-line frequencies ([Sun 2020](https://dcc.ligo.org/public/0162/P1900245/007/CalO3.pdf); [O4 cal, arXiv:2508.08423](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08423)), each given its own best amplitude allocation? The optimal scheme balances the drive so the worst parameter governs. The LIGO placements measure sensing (`κ_C`, `f_cc`), `δ`, `τ` and the test-mass strength `κ_TST` quickly, but spend far longer on the **top-mass `κ_M0` and penultimate `κ_PUM`** strengths — their actuator lines sit at ~15–35 Hz, where those slow stages have little DARM authority, so the ruler `κ_i·D_i·N_i` is small and the SNR low (`κ_M0` is the binding parameter for both O3 and O4 here). ::: {#14fc119b .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Time to 0.1% per parameter — P&S-optimal vs O3 vs O4"} dd.scheme_bars_fig(sz) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#2ed7836b .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Time to 0.1% on all seven, and the speed-up"} display(dd.sizing_table(sz)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Time for every TDCF to reach 0.1% at equal total drive. The advantage is concentrated in δ and τ (which LIGO monitors but does not correct to 0.1%); for the κ's the schemes are comparable. Absolute times are representative (drive-match deferred); the ratio is scale-invariant.** | line scheme | time to 0.1% on all 7 [s] | binding param | vs P&S-optimal | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | P&S-optimal | 90 | delta | 1.0× | | LIGO O3 lines | 2543 | kappa_M0 | 28.3× | | LIGO O4 lines | 3919 | kappa_M0 | 43.5× | ::: ::: The advantage is concentrated in the **hierarchical actuation strengths `κ_M0` and `κ_PUM`**: the P&S scheme places each actuator line in its stage's authority band (M0 low, PUM mid), while the O3/O4 lines share a mid-band (~15–35 Hz) actuator region where the upper stages are weak. Part of this is a genuine SNR effect — top-mass authority rolls off steeply — and part is a **stage-set caveat**: the twin actuates M0/PUM/ESD, while O3/O4 actuate UIM/PUM/TST, so mapping their line frequencies onto this hierarchy penalises the upper stages more than it would in the real instrument. For sensing (`κ_C`, `f_cc`), `δ`, `τ` and `κ_TST` the schemes are within a factor of a few. The absolute times are representative (only the total drive is borrowed from the papers; matching the exact per-line amplitudes and the full O4 line list is the next phase); the **ratio** is scale-invariant. ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"} ## Calibration team: help us make this exact The comparison above uses the real O3/O4 line *frequencies* but a single **representative** total drive — we do not yet have the actual per-line amplitudes. **If you work on LIGO calibration, we'd love the real cal-line heights in physical units** (Pcal displacement amplitudes [m]; per-stage UIM/PUM/TST actuator drives [counts / N / m]; the integration convention behind the quoted TDCF uncertainties; and the full O4 line list). Drop them into [**issue #3**](https://github.com/CaltechExperimentalGravity/system_ident/issues/3) — a comment or a PR — and we'll fold them into the simulation for a fully apples-to-apples, absolute comparison. Only published / DCC numbers are needed (nothing embargoed). ::: ## Reaching the O3/O4 random-error levels — gently and fast The published response budget has two parts: a **systematic** error (from imperfect modelling) and a **random** (statistical) uncertainty (from the finite-SNR line measurements). This scheme attacks the *random* part — that is what more/gentler line SNR buys. Propagating the cal-line CRB (the full 7-parameter covariance `Σ = Γ⁻¹` through `∂lnR/∂lnθ`, with the digital servo `D` held fixed so a κ_i error moves `A`→`R` exactly as the real pipeline does) gives the statistical response uncertainty `δR/R(f)`. The reference levels come from O3 ([Sun 2020](https://dcc.ligo.org/public/0162/P1900245/007/CalO3.pdf)): total error + uncertainty **< 7% / < 4°** (68% CI, 20–2000 Hz) and systematic error alone **< 2% / < 2°**, so the **O3 random level** is their quadrature difference, **≈ 6.7% / 3.5°**. (The O3 systematic floor, 2% / 2°, serves as a provisional **O4-class** aspiration — the final O4 budget is [forthcoming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08423).) ::: {#e0739d37 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="δR/R(f) from the cal-line CRB vs the O3 budget levels"} dd.response_budget_fig(sz) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The response uncertainty falls as `1/√(amplitude²·time)`, so reaching a target random-error level costs a fixed **injected energy** `A²·T`, and the amplitude↔time trade is a **Pareto slider**. The key result: a **response-optimal** P&S scheme (drive split to minimise `δR/R`, not the worst single parameter) reaches a given level with far less energy than the fixed-line or naive schemes — so you can run **gentler** (less amplitude on the mirrors) or **faster** (less time), your choice. ::: {#ec14ddb5 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Amplitude↔time Pareto — P&S response-optimal vs O3/O4 fixed-line and naive"} pc = dd.pareto_campaign(seed=0) dd.pareto_fig(pc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#7337852c .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Injected-energy savings to reach each random-error level"} display(dd.pareto_table(pc)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Injected energy A²·T to reach each random-error level: P&S response-optimal vs the O3/O4 fixed-line and naive-broadband schemes. The energy saving converts to √(factor)× less amplitude (at equal time) or factor× less time (at equal amplitude). Ratios are scale-invariant; absolute amplitude awaits real line heights (issue #3).** | random-error target | |δR/R| level | energy vs fixed-line | energy vs naive | → less amplitude / less time (vs fixed) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | O3 random | 6.7% / 3.5° | 18.1× | 3681.3× | 4.3× / 18× | | O4-class (prov.) | 2% / 2° | 18.1× | 3681.3× | 4.3× / 18× | | 0.1% stretch | 0.1% / 0.1° | 18.1× | 3681.3× | 4.3× / 18× | ::: ::: To reach the **O3 random level**, the P&S scheme needs **~18× less injected energy than the O3/O4 fixed-line placement** (≈4× less amplitude at equal time, or ~18× less time at equal amplitude) and **>1000× less than a naive broadband injection** — the same factor at every target level, down to the 0.1% stretch. Slide along a contour to trade drive for time and design the campaign. (Absolute amplitudes await the real per-line heights — [issue #3](https://github.com/CaltechExperimentalGravity/system_ident/issues/3); the *ratios* here are scale-invariant. Systematic modelling errors — the 0.54% Pcal reference, unmodelled low-frequency response, actuator-model error — are a separate axis this twin does not address.) ## Head-to-head with the swept sine Same twin, same disturbance + readout noise, same total wall-clock. The multisine measures every bin at once; the swept sine spends the clock one frequency at a time, so in equal time it reaches only a handful of frequencies (each tight, because it spends full power there) — and covering the whole band to the same uncertainty costs it ~100× longer. Shown on the same twin, not asserted. ::: {#18a6c830 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="σ(R)/|R| — multisine (whole band) vs swept sine (few points), equal wall-clock"} c = dd.comparison(seed=0) dd.comparison_fig(c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#34495863 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Where the methods differ"} display(dd.fom_table(c)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Where the multisine method differs for DARM (representative; the efficiency is shown above, not asserted)** | figure of merit | swept sine | P&S multisine | | --- | --- | --- | | Frequencies per measurement | 1 (dwell) | all band bins at once | | Leakage | windowed / settle each point | leakage-free (periodic) | | Noise model | assumed / averaged | per-bin, from period-to-period variance | | Budget allocation | uniform / manual | CRB-optimal (Fisher-matched) | | Loop handling | model out the servo | FRF cancels it (reference-based) | | Time for full-band coverage | ≈99 min | 16 s (one window) | ::: ::: ## Honest gaps This twin is a single DARM loop with the coupled detuned-cavity sensing (the SRC-detuning `δ` splits the cavity pole into a complex pair). It shows leakage-free recovery of `C`, the per-stage strengths and their CRB convergence, the hierarchical actuation crossovers, the cal-line SNR budget, and a Fisher-optimal line design benchmarked against O3/O4 — but it still holds the parameters static within a record (drift is tracked in [example 13](13-darm-drift-tracking.qmd)), and omits the cross-couplings of a real interferometer. The noise floor and line SNRs are *representative*, not a specific instrument state, and the O3/O4 comparison borrows only the total drive (exact per-line amplitudes / the full O4 line list are the next phase); the real test is to run these injections on the same instrument and compare the `σ(R(f))`-per-hour envelopes — see `notes/darm-calibration-via-pns.md`. ## Roadmap The through-line never changes — a periodic multisine, a leakage-free reference FRF, a maximum-likelihood fit toward the Cramér–Rao bound. Each step below raises the *twin's* fidelity toward a real DARM calibration, keeping that one method. **Done** - **Static single-loop calibration** (this page). Sensing `C`, three-stage actuation `κ`, the response `R(f)` with a measured CRB envelope, and a swept-sine head-to-head on the same twin. - **Round 1 — track a drifting parameter** ([example 13](13-darm-drift-tracking.qmd)). A known slow drift on the ESD strength `κ(t)`, recovered with a Lataire–Pintelon time-basis fit inside an honest CRB band, with resolvability proven by a computed bound rather than eyeballed. **Next — raising fidelity, roughly in order** 1. **Realistic drift** — replace the deterministic profile with a stochastic (GP) wander at a physical correlation time; score the recovery statistically. 2. **SRC-detuning optical spring** — replace the single real sensing pole with an optical biquad parametrized on the physical detuning `φ`, so the DARM pole migrates **real → complex** as `φ` drifts (the crossing stays analytic in `φ`). 3. **Several parameters at once** — the optical gain, the cavity-pole / detuning, and the stage `κ_i` drifting jointly, not one scalar in isolation. 4. **One-shot Lataire–Pintelon fit** — fit the time-basis coefficients directly to the record, alongside today's two-step snapshot form, as a cross-check. 5. **Continuous TDCF lines** — always-on calibration lines tracking `κ(t)` between full sweeps, the operational counterpart to the snapshot campaign. 6. **The actuation / DAC chain** — whitening / de-whitening and coil-driver shaping with a pre-injection saturation check at the DAC, plus ESD charge / voltage limits. 7. **Real filters & couplings** — import real DARM / actuation filter shapes and the interferometer cross-couplings (MIMO), toward a calibration of an actual instrument state. Live-CDS / hardware injection is a separate, later phase. The full design and citations live in `notes/darm-calibration-via-pns.md`.
